chapterTitle: Chapter 5 — How Models Are Built and Run
instructions: Analyze this chapter segment faithfully. Capture its thesis, role, ideas, representative evidence, objections, and qualifications. Cite source unit IDs.

units.text: Finally, cost, which is the arithmetic of running a model, multiplied. Every training step carries the memory and the threefold compute counted for the two lives of a model, and a frontier model takes an enormous number of steps. In practice that means thousands to tens of thousands of graphics cards running for weeks to months. Companies rarely publish the bills, but independent estimates for the largest runs are in the tens of millions of dollars and climbing toward hundreds of millions, while adapting a modest model with LoRA can cost less than a dinner. Energy follows the same curve. One widely cited estimate, by Google researchers in 2021, put the training of GPT-3 at about 1,300 megawatt-hours, roughly what a hundred and twenty American homes use in a year, and frontier runs since then have been much larger. A single answer is small by comparison: in 2025 Google reported that a median text prompt to its Gemini assistant used about a quarter of a watt-hour, comparable to about nine seconds of television, though such figures depend heavily on what is counted and are hard to check from outside. Multiplied by billions of requests, plus the water that cools the data centers, the total becomes a matter for power grids and town councils rather than for one engineering team.

So “how much is enough?” has an honest answer, though not a single number: enough is where your learning curve flattens, measured on your own data, with duplicates removed and the hard cases covered. Past that point you need a better teacher, not more practice. With that, the engine room tour is over. Before we turn to language and meaning, though, one question has been waiting patiently since the start of the previous chapter. If a network is not a brain, then what is a brain, the one that runs on twenty watts and learns as it goes, actually doing? Neuroscience has some bold answers, and the boldest of them begins with a coffee cup.

Going further. If you wondered what actually happens inside a language model as it writes one token after another, section 7.3 walks through it frame by frame. How a finished model goes back to school for a narrower job, from transfer learning to LoRA, is the subject of section 9.2. The crammer you built, its opposite the slacker, and the remaining cures for both have section 10.1 to themselves. And how sure a model really is, when it answers every question with the same fluent assurance, is the question of section 10.5.
